# Ezekiel 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview and Structure

The chapter is widely seen as having three sections: (1) judgment against the high places of idolatry (vv. 1–7), (2) the promise of a spared remnant (vv. 8–10), and (3) a call to lament combined with the announcement of total desolation (vv. 11–14). Matthew Henry calls this "a threatening of the destruction of Israel for their idolatry, and the destruction of their idols with them" followed by "a promise of the gracious return of a remnant." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill notes that the prophecy covers "the desolation of the whole land of Israel, and a promise that a remnant should escape, with a lamentation for the sad destruction, signified by some gestures of the prophet." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 1: "And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,"

A standard prophetic formula. Ezekiel claims direct divine revelation. Gill notes that according to Junius this was delivered "on a sabbath day, the twenty first of the fifth month, in the sixth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity" — over a year after the vision at Chebar (Ezekiel 1:1). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes this asserts Ezekiel's "claim to inspiration or Divine revelation of what he had to say and write, 2 Peter 1:21." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 2: "Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them."

**Traditional reading**: The "mountains of Israel" refers to the land of Palestine generally (not just the northern ten tribes). JFB explains that the mountains are addressed by personification "implying that the Israelites themselves are incurable and unworthy of any more appeals" — much as the prophet sent to Jeroboam addressed the altar rather than the king (1 Kings 13:2). The mountains are specified as "the scene of Jewish idolatries on 'the high places'" (Leviticus 26:30). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Guzik adds: "This prophecy was directed against the mountains because they helped define the geography of Israel, and more importantly, they were centers of idol worship – the infamous high places mentioned many times in the Old Testament." He cites Wright: "Probably in any part of Palestine at this time you would have found some mountain or hill crowned with an altar, one or two standing stones, a wooden pillar, and a clump of evergreen trees." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

Gill notes that the mountains are called to hear the word partly "to show the stupidity of the Jews...that it was as well, or better, to speak to the mountains, than to them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary adds that "the Lord has a controversy with the mountains and their prominent physical features, as if they had ears and faculties for understanding. He, as it were, directs His admonitions through them to the men who had disordered those features by setting up forbidden idols." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 3: "O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! … I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places."

**The high places (bamot)**: Precept Austin provides an extensive study showing that high places were associated with at least six activities: burning incense, sacrificing, eating sacrificial meals, praying, prostitution, and child sacrifice. The "sad refrain" in 2 Kings — "only the high places were not taken away" — is noted seven times; if Israel would not destroy the high places, God would. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_61-7)

Guzik notes that "altars to pagan gods were often set on the tops of hills and mountains in ancient Israel and the broader region. This idolatry on the high places was inherited from the Canaanites." He adds: "To the ravines, and to the valleys: 'There must have been some similar worship in the ravines and valleys (Isaiah 57:5,6; Jeremiah 2:23; 7:31), perhaps sometimes cave worship of an earth-mother, or, as Isaiah and Jeremiah suggest, child sacrifice.'" (Wright) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

JFB notes that "rivers" (literally "channels of torrents") were "often the scene and objects of idolatrous worship." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Matthew Henry, quoted by Precept Austin, writes: "God sometimes ruins idolatries even by the hands of idolaters, for such the Chaldeans themselves were... It is just with God to make that a desolation which we make an idol of." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_61-7)

---

## v. 4: "Your altars will be demolished and your incense altars will be smashed; and I will cast down your slain before your idols."

**"Your altars"**: Matthew Poole is cited by Guzik pointing out that God calls them "your altars" — "God's altar was only at Jerusalem, these were their altars." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

**"Images" / incense altars**: The Hebrew word for "images" (chammanim) is connected by JFB to a root meaning "to wax hot," implying "the mad ardor of Israel after idolatry" (per Calvin). Others translate it as "sun images" (see 2 Kings 23:11; Isaiah 17:8, margin). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill similarly notes the word "has its derivation from heat; and were so called, either from the heat of the sun, to whose worship they were devoted, or from the heat of the love and affections of their worshippers." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

**"Slain before your idols"**: Gill notes the word for idols (gillulim) here has "the signification of dung" (see Ezekiel 4:12) — "dunghill gods." The Targum renders it "before the carcass of your idols." The point is that where they committed idolatry, there they would be slain. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary notes: "It is probably connected with a root which signifies filth, and is a contemptuous description of them — they are dung, or refuse-gods." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 5: "I will lay the corpses of the Israelites before their idols and scatter your bones around your altars."

**Pollution of the altars**: JFB says this means "polluting thus with the dead bones of you, the worshippers, the idols which seemed to you so sacrosanct." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Guzik cites Feinberg: "Because the land had been defiled by idols, the idols themselves would now be defiled by the corpses of the worshipers, a retribution in kind. This would be the height of desecration, replacing the fragrance of incense with the odor of putrefaction." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

Gill notes that scattered bones "were reckoned a pollution" of altars, citing 2 Kings 23:14 where Josiah defiled altars with human bones. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

Guzik also cites Clarke: "This was literally fulfilled by the Chaldeans. According to Baruch, Bar 2:24, 25, they opened the sepulchres of the principal people, and threw the bones about on every side." The "scattering of bones" is a phrase used for judgment conveying uncleanness and shame (cf. Psalm 53:5; 141:7). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary paints the graphic scene: "their bones to be bleached by the burning sun, as a testimony of the vanity of falling down before idols." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 6: "Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste and the high places will be demolished … your works blotted out."

**Universal desolation**: Gill notes "the desolation should be general, wherever they had cities and places to dwell in; the idolatry being universal, as is said in Jeremiah 2:28." The phrase "your works may be abolished" refers not only to the works of their hands but "of their brain; whatever they had devised, and was contrary to the pure word and worship of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

JFB notes: "your works — not gods, as you supposed, but the mere work of men's hands (Isaiah 40:18–20)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Guzik: "The armies of Babylon would destroy both the cities and the country regions." He cites Poole: "Desolate; no priest to attend, no sacrifice offered, nor a votary come to them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

---

## v. 7: "The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD."

**The recognition formula**: This is the first occurrence in Ezekiel of the phrase "you will know that I am the LORD," repeated some sixty times in the book. Guzik cites Smith: "This so-called recognition formula, which occurs some sixty times in the book, captures the theme of this prophet. God's motive in all that he does is that he might be recognized as the only God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

JFB: "Ye shall know Me as the all-powerful Punisher of sin" — "and not your idols, lords." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary notes the word "slain" is singular in Hebrew, "as if to show that one mind had animated the mass of the slain in practising idolatry." There will be survivors "to see the slaughtered idolaters, and the eye will affect their heart so that they shall recognise the action of the almighty, righteous One." Thus "a ground is laid for the following promise." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 8: "Yet I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the nations and throughout the lands."

**The remnant motif**: Guzik connects this to "the acted-out parable of the cut hair (Ezekiel 5:3-4)." He says God "specifically promised to leave a remnant that would be the basis of a later restoration." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

JFB calls this a "mitigation of the extreme severity of their punishment; still their life shall be a wretched one, and linked with exile (Ezekiel 5:2, 12; 12:16; 14:22; Jeremiah 44:28)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Matthew Henry: "Judgment had hitherto triumphed, but in these verses mercy rejoices against judgment. A sad end is made of this provoking people, but not a full end." He emphasizes that "God's patience both leaves room for repentance and is an encouragement to sinners to repent." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill: the remnant is "not in Judea, but in Babylon, and in the countries where they should be dispersed." He says the scattering would be into "Egypt, Ammon, Moab, and Assyria; for this respects their dispersion at the time of the Babylonish captivity, and not their present dispersion." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

Wiersbe (quoted in Precept Austin): "In grace, God would spare a remnant that would remember Him and repent of their sins. The sin that breaks the heart of God should break our hearts as well." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_68-14)

---

## v. 9: "Then in the nations … your survivors will remember Me—how I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts … So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations."

**"I am broken" / "I have been grieved"**: The Hebrew is intensely personal. Guzik calls this "a startling statement. Using a human analogy, God expressed the depth of the grief He felt over Israel's idolatry by likening Himself to a husband with a constantly unfaithful wife." He cites G. Campbell Morgan: "The strongest figure possible is used to portray the Divine suffering. God is represented as broken." And F.B. Meyer: "Our sin can give God the heartbreak, because He loves us so. Indeed, on the Cross the Lord died of a broken heart." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

JFB discusses the translation debate: "Fairbairn translates, actively, 'I will break' their whorish heart; English Version is better. In their exile they shall remember how long I bore with them, but was at last compelled to punish, after I was 'broken' (My long-suffering wearied out) by their desperate spiritual whorishness [Calvin]." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill offers two senses: "either that he was grieved at heart with their idolatry, which was the reason of their being carried captive...or that he was full of compassion towards them; his heart was tender and pitiful towards them." The Targum renders it "I have broken their foolish heart" (active), while Syriac and Vulgate also take it actively. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

**"Idols" (gillulim)**: Guzik notes the word is a favourite with Ezekiel (38 times vs. 9 times in the rest of the OT). Taylor explains it is "a home-made word consisting of the vowels of Hebrew siqqus ('detested thing') and the consonants of a noun meaning 'a pellet of dung'. The final combination carries about as much disdain and revulsion as any word could do." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

**"Loathe themselves"**: JFB says "they shall not wait for men to condemn them but shall condemn themselves" (cf. Ezekiel 20:43; 36:31; Job 42:6; 1 Corinthians 11:31). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Guzik cites Trapp: "They shall bleed inwardly, and blush outwardly, deeply detesting their former abominations." He adds that Matthew Poole notes they "would loathe themselves for all their abominations, not merely some of them. 'It is a hypocrite's repentance which is but for some; this of the reserved remnant shall be sound.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

Matthew Henry illustrates the process: "They shall remember me. Note, To those whom God designs for life he will give repentance unto life... Where God designs grace to repent he allows space to repent." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/6.htm)

---

## v. 10: "And they will know that I am the LORD; I did not declare in vain that I would bring this calamity upon them."

**God's word not in vain**: Gill interprets "in vain" either as God speaking within His own purposes and decrees (so the Targum: "I have not in vain decreed in my word") or through the prophets' mouths. The "evil" here is "not the evil of sin, but the evil of punishment, or of affliction." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

Guzik sees a progression: "Remembrance of God → Repentance from sin → Relationship restored." He cites Block: "The escapees will emerge from their dispersal among the nations a transformed people... The future lay with the exiles." And Clarke: "Those that escape the sword...shall plainly see that it is God who has done this, and shall humble themselves on account of their abominations, leave their idolatry, and worship Him alone. And this they have done from the Babylonish captivity to the present day." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary notes the wording should be read: "And they shall know that I the Lord have not said in vain that I would do this evil unto them." The point is not merely that they know He is the living God but that He was "true to all His warnings." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 11: "Clap your hands, stomp your feet, and cry out 'Alas!' because of all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel, who will fall by sword and famine and plague."

**The gestures**: JFB explains these are "gesticulations vividly setting before the hearers the greatness of the calamity about to be inflicted. In indignation at the abominations of Israel extend thine hand towards Judea, as if about to 'strike,' and 'stamp,' shaking off the dust with thy foot, in token of how God shall 'stretch out His hand upon them,' and tread them down (Ezekiel 6:14; 21:14)." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill says these are "gestures of persons in distress and agony, who, to show their trouble and grief, smite one hand against the other; or smite with the hand upon the thigh, as in Jeremiah 31:19." He notes the Hebrew for "stamp" literally means "make a distension with the foot" — extending the thighs, throwing out the feet, stamping, beating the earth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

Guzik cites Vawter and Hoppe: "'Clap your hands, and stamp your foot' are instructions that intend both to draw attention and to convey a premonition of threat and defiance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

**Sword, famine, plague**: The same threefold judgment as in Ezekiel 5:12. Guzik cites Feinberg: "Emphatic warning was directed to them in the light of the three dread calamities predicted: sword, famine and pestilence. There would be no escape when these somber horsemen began their ride of death." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes these judgments "fell not only on the city of Jerusalem but also upon all the house of Israel." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 12: "He who is far off will die by the plague, he who is near will fall by the sword, and he who remains will die by famine. So I will vent My fury upon them."

**No escape**: JFB distinguishes: "He that is far off — namely, from the foe; those who in a distant exile fear no evil. He that remaineth — he that is left in the city; not carried away into captivity, nor having escaped into the country. Distinct from 'he that is near,' namely, those outside the city who are within reach of 'the sword' of the foe, and so fall by it; not by 'famine,' as those left in the city." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill: "He that is far off shall die of the pestilence, that flies from the enemy into the wilderness, or into other countries, thinking himself safe there, the plague shall seize him, and he shall die of that; there is no fleeing from God, and escaping his hand." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

**"Accomplish my fury"**: Gill explains that wrath had been "gradually, by little and little, falling upon them, in order to bring them to repentance; but being incorrigible, wrath is brought upon them to the uttermost; and God fulfils the whole counsel of his will in their destruction." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 13: "Then you will know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, and under every green tree and leafy oak — the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols."

**Idolatry's geography**: Gill notes the listing of locations matches the practices of the heathen, citing Herodotus: "the Persians, that, going up to the highest parts of mountains, they offered sacrifice to Jupiter." In "righteous judgment, here their carcasses should fill and lie, and rot and stink" — where they offered sweet savour, there their corpses would stink. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

Guzik: "The fulfillment of these prophecies would demonstrate to Israel that Yahweh was their God, and worthy of their repentance. They would (and did) reject their idols after these severe judgments." He adds that God called the idols "your idols" — "the gods they cried to could not defend from death, and, their nothingness having been proved, they would be defiled by the corpses of their unhelped devotees." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasizes the "testamentary evidence" — the living remnant would see the slain among the idols and know that the Lord was God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-6.html)

---

## v. 14: "I will stretch out My hand against them, and wherever they live I will make the land a desolate waste, from the wilderness to Diblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

**"Stretch out My hand"**: Guzik cites Poole: "This noteth the greatness of the blow, God striketh hard when he stretcheth out his hand, and therefore you find a mighty hand joined with outstretched arm." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

**"Diblah" (or Riblah)**: There is a textual issue here. Guzik explains: "There are some ancient texts that read Riblah instead of Diblah. This may be due to an error in copying the text... the exact meaning or place of Diblah is unknown." Vawter and Hoppe (cited by Guzik): "This is undoubtedly due to a scribal confusion of the Hebrew letters 'd' and 'r.'" Riblah was "the fateful site where Nebuchadnezzar would seal the doom of Jerusalem and Judah after the debacle of 587/6 (2 Kings 25:20–21)." Wiersbe (also cited): "God promised to devastate the land 'from the desert to Riblah [Diblah]' (NIV), that is, from the south to the north. It's like saying 'from Dan to Beersheba,' from the north to the south." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

JFB identifies Diblath as "another form of Diblathaim, a city in Moab (Numbers 33:46; Jeremiah 48:22), near which, east and south of the Dead Sea, was the wilderness of Arabia-Deserta." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

Gill notes Kimchi and Ben Melech think Diblath is the same as Riblath (as Deuel/Reuel in Numbers 1:14), in the land of Hamath — where Nebuchadnezzar brought Zedekiah and slew his sons before him (Jeremiah 39:5). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

**The final recognition formula**: Guzik closes citing Taylor: "The words typify Ezekiel's message and longing, that Yahweh may be known by all men, Israelite and non-Israelite, for what he is—the one true God, the God of the world, the God of history, the God who speaks and does not speak in vain." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

---

## Traditions and Theological Distinctives

### Baptist Perspective

The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasises the evangelistic purpose in the judgment — that the scattered bones would serve "as a testimony of the vanity of falling down before idols" — and sees the remnant promise as fulfilled in believers across all ages (citing Romans 11:5). It ties the loathing to realizing that "their idolatry had been as loathsome to their God as incurable leprosy is to people of health." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-6.html)

Gill (a Baptist of an earlier era, 1746) provides detailed Hebrew word studies, noting the derivation of key terms (gillulim = dung-gods, chammanim = sun-images/heat), and stresses that the Babylonian captivity cured Israel of idolatry. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-6.html)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic Perspective (Enduring Word, David Guzik)

Guzik's commentary (Enduring Word) is broadly evangelical but with Pentecostal/charismatic associations. Distinctive emphases include: the personal, emotional suffering of God ("I was crushed" — God as a brokenhearted husband), and the strong pastoral application. He draws heavily on G. Campbell Morgan and F.B. Meyer, who both emphasize the cross — "on the Cross the Lord died of a broken heart." The recognition formula in v. 7 is highlighted as the book's great theme. The commentary also gives attention to the "acted-out parable" nature of Ezekiel's ministry (clapping, stamping), consistent with charismatic openness to embodied prophetic action. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)

### Reformed Perspective (JFB)

JFB emphasises God's sovereignty in judgment: the destruction is God's own work ("I, even I, will bring a sword"). The commentary sees partial fulfillment in the eradication of idolatry after the Babylonian captivity but also a future, fuller fulfillment: "But they have yet to repent of their crowning sin, the crucifixion of Messiah; their full repentance is therefore future, after the ordeal of trials for many centuries, ending with that foretold in Zechariah 10:9; 13:8,9; 14:1-4,11." This reflects a historic Reformed premillennialism that sees ongoing significance for ethnic Israel. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/6.htm)

---

## Other Views / Modern Scholarship

**Textual note on v. 14 (Diblah/Riblah)**: As noted above from Guzik citing Vawter and Hoppe: the received Hebrew text reads "Diblah," but this "is undoubtedly due to a scribal confusion of the Hebrew letters 'd' and 'r,' a thing that has occurred several times over in the transmission of the biblical text." Riblah in Syria was the site where Nebuchadnezzar executed Zedekiah's sons and blinded him (2 Kings 25:20-21), making it a highly significant name for Ezekiel's exilic audience. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-6/)
